title: Anytime-CBU: Adaptive Rollout Allocation for Consequence-Based Utility Scoring

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The purpose of the contribution is to reduce the computational cost of Consequence-Based Utility (CBU) scoring by avoiding wasteful compute on candidates whose quality is clear after few rollouts. None of the prior papers explicitly address this specific problem of optimizing CBU scoring or reducing its computational cost. While some papers (e.g., [6], [9], [10]) discuss test-time compute optimization for LLMs, they do not target the specific inefficiency in CBU scoring or propose solutions tailored to this problem. Therefore, no prior paper contains a substantively equivalent purpose.

### Mechanism
The mechanism reformulates CBU scoring as a best-arm identification (BAI) problem and applies LUCB-style adaptive allocation with Beta-posterior confidence bounds, arm elimination, and early stopping. Several prior papers ([1], [4], [5], [7], [22]) discuss LUCB-style algorithms or related BAI techniques, including adaptive allocation, confidence bounds, and arm elimination. For example, [1] introduces LUCB-H with adaptive confidence bounds, [4] applies Bayesian fixed-confidence BAI, and [7] uses LUCB with arm elimination. These mechanisms are substantively equivalent to the core technical primitives of Anytime-CBU, even though the application context differs.

### Evaluation
The evaluation uses RealMath with two solver models (Qwen2.5-Math-7B and DeepSeek-R1-7B) against Uniform-CBU. While the specific benchmark (RealMath) and models are new, the evaluation design — comparing an adaptive allocation method against a uniform baseline in a test-time compute optimization context — is not novel. Papers like [6], [9], and [10] evaluate adaptive test-time compute strategies using similar designs, albeit with different benchmarks and models. For example, [9] evaluates compute efficiency in reasoning tasks, and [10] compares adaptive compute allocation against fixed strategies. Thus, the evaluation design is covered.

### Domain
The domain is LLM evaluation and test-time compute optimization for mathematical reasoning. Papers like [6], [9], and [10] also operate in the domain of LLM test-time compute optimization, including reasoning tasks. While the specific focus on mathematical reasoning (RealMath) is narrower, it falls within the broader domain of LLM evaluation and compute optimization. Therefore, the domain is covered.

The purpose is to empirically validate whether an adaptive (anytime) allocation strategy achieves its promised computational savings compared to uniform allocation, specifically for CBU (Confidence-Based Uncertainty) scoring. Paper [2] "LLM-as-Judge on a Budget" addresses variance-adaptive query allocation for LLM evaluation and studies whether adaptive allocation improves estimation efficiency. Still, [9] and [14] are substantively equivalent in purpose: comparing adaptive vs. uniform allocation to assess cost reduction.

The specific finding (near-zero savings) is the novel substance, but the evaluation design (CI-based comparison of adaptive vs. uniform) is covered by [2].
